summary.text: The Paleocene–Eocene thermal maximum was a geologically brief interval about 56 million years ago when global average temperature rose 5–8 °C as huge amounts of carbon entered the ocean and atmosphere.
It lasted about 200,000 years and is arguably the best past example for understanding how global warming and the carbon cycle work in a greenhouse world.
Its mark appears at hundreds of sites worldwide as a large drop in the ¹³C/¹²C ratio of carbonates and organic carbon, alongside major turnovers in fossil records.

items.prompt: Rock and sediment layers at hundreds of sites around the world all show the same sudden fall in carbon-13 compared with carbon-12. What does that worldwide signal mainly record?

options.label: A huge release of carbon into sea and air
A spread of ice sheets across both poles
A sudden fall in global sea level
A burst of radiation from a nearby star

items.explain: The drop in the ¹³C/¹²C ratio, found and matched across hundreds of locations, is evidence of a massive release of carbon to the ocean and atmosphere.

items.prompt: Why do climate scientists keep returning to an event from 56 million years ago?

options.label: It marks the moment the dinosaurs died out
It may be the best past guide to greenhouse warming
It was the coldest stretch in 60 million years
It built the first ice sheets on Antarctica

items.explain: The PETM is arguably the best past analogue for how global warming and the carbon cycle operate in a greenhouse world.

items.prompt: Around the start of the PETM, fossils on land in Europe and North America change abruptly. What shows up?

options.label: The first flowering plants
The last of the giant dinosaurs
Many modern mammal orders, primates included
The earliest four-legged animals

items.explain: On land, many modern mammal orders, including primates, suddenly appear in Europe and North America.

items.prompt: If you could sail into the central Arctic Ocean during the PETM, what would you find?

options.label: A thick cap of year-round sea ice
Sea ice in winter that melted each summer
Glaciers calving icebergs into the water
Open water with no ice on it

items.explain: The central Arctic Ocean was ice-free before, during and after the PETM, and there was no significant sea ice at the time.

items.prompt: Shells of tiny sea creatures show an oxygen-isotope shift across the PETM. Such a shift can mean either that more water was locked up frozen on land, or that seawater warmed. Why is it read as warming here?

options.label: Only shells from the sea surface were sampled
Oxygen in shells responds only to heat
Little or no polar ice existed back then
The shells all came from freshwater lakes

items.explain: Because there was little or no polar ice in the early Paleogene, the oxygen-isotope shift in surface and deep-water shells very probably means the ocean got warmer.

items.prompt: The PETM is one of several 'hyperthermals': geologically brief events with rapid warming and massive carbon addition. What sets it apart from the rest?

options.label: It was the most extreme of them
It was the first one in the Cenozoic
It was the only one in the tropics
It lasted for several million years

items.explain: Though not the first in the Cenozoic, the PETM was the most extreme hyperthermal, and it lasted about 200,000 years, not millions.

paragraphs.heading: A sudden hot spell
paragraphs.text: About 56 million years ago, Earth went through a burst of warming now called the Paleocene–Eocene thermal maximum, or PETM. Average temperature across the globe climbed by 5–8 °C, while an enormous amount of carbon poured into the ocean and the air. The event sits exactly on the line between two geological epochs, the Paleocene and the Eocene. By the standards of geology it was short: it lasted about 200,000 years.

paragraphs.heading: Why scientists care
paragraphs.text: The PETM is arguably the best case from Earth's past for learning how global warming and the carbon cycle behave in a greenhouse world. Yet much is still uncertain. How big the carbon release was, exactly when it happened, and where all that carbon came from are still being actively researched.

paragraphs.heading: A fingerprint in carbon
paragraphs.text: The event leaves a clear mark in the rocks: a large fall in the ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12. This fall shows up in carbonates and organic carbon, both from the sea and from land. It has been found and matched up at hundreds of places around the world. Over recent decades, rock layers spanning the event have shown that far more changed than temperature and carbon.

paragraphs.heading: How we know it got hotter
paragraphs.text: Estimates of the warming at the start of the event run from about 3–6 °C up to 5–8 °C. Several kinds of evidence agree. The shells of foraminifera from both surface and deep water show a clear shift in their oxygen isotopes, written δ¹⁸O. With little or no polar ice around at the time, that shift most likely means the ocean warmed. Warmth-loving species spreading to higher latitudes and changes in the shape and size of leaves back this up.

paragraphs.heading: Hot seas
paragraphs.text: One chemical measure suggests tropical sea surfaces averaged over 36 °C. That was hot enough to stress even hardy organisms such as dinoflagellates, and a large number of their species died out. Oxygen isotope data from Tanzania hint that tropical waters may have passed 40 °C. In the North Sea, surface temperatures leapt by 10 °C to around 33 °C. The central Arctic Ocean had no ice before, during or after the event.

paragraphs.heading: Life turned over
paragraphs.text: Fossils show major turnovers in many groups of living things, as fits the boundary between two epochs. In the oceans, benthic foraminifera suffered a mass extinction, subtropical dinoflagellates spread across the globe, and new excursion forms appeared among planktic foraminifera and calcareous nannofossils. On land, many modern orders of mammals, primates among them, suddenly turn up in Europe and North America.

paragraphs.heading: One of several hot spikes
paragraphs.text: The PETM was not alone. From the late Paleocene into the early Eocene, Earth slowly warmed by about 6 °C, and on top of that slow rise came at least three shorter events called hyperthermals. A hyperthermal is a brief episode, under 200,000 years, of fast global warming, big environmental change and a huge addition of carbon. The PETM was the most extreme of them, though not the first in the Cenozoic.
